questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A patient suddenly becomes unresponsive with bilateral tonic-clonic movements. Which observation should the RN record immediately?
choices: Only whether incontinence occurs
The exact start time and sequence of movements, breathing, and responsiveness
An assumed diagnosis of lifelong epilepsy
A conclusion that the event is harmless if it ends
questions.explanation: The start time and clinical sequence guide recognition of prolonged seizures and treatment response. Breathing, responsiveness, and injury risk must be assessed alongside the movements.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: During a generalized convulsion, which action best protects the patient?
choices: Hold both arms and legs firmly still
Place a padded spoon between the teeth
Give water to prevent dehydration
Clear hazards, cushion the head, and turn the person to the side when safe
questions.explanation: Seizure first aid protects against injury and supports airway drainage. Restraining movements or placing objects in the mouth can cause harm.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A bilateral convulsion has continued for 5 minutes. What is the priority?
choices: Activate the status epilepticus response and prepare ordered rescue treatment while supporting ABCs
Wait until 30 minutes to decide whether it is an emergency
Offer oral antiseizure tablets during active convulsions
Leave the room to avoid overstimulation
questions.explanation: A generalized convulsion lasting about 5 minutes requires immediate emergency treatment. Airway and circulation support, glucose testing, and ordered benzodiazepine rescue proceed in parallel.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Two seizures occur close together and the patient never regains consciousness between them. Which interpretation is safest?
choices: Recovery is complete between events
The second seizure proves medication toxicity only
This can represent status epilepticus even if each individual episode is short
No emergency response is needed without incontinence
questions.explanation: Repeated convulsions without return to baseline are a status epilepticus pattern and require urgent treatment and monitoring, independent of incontinence.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which medication class is usually first-line for ongoing convulsive status epilepticus under an emergency protocol?
choices: Oral statins
Benzodiazepines by an authorized route
Routine antibiotics without evidence of infection
Long-term maintenance medicine given only after discharge
questions.explanation: Guidelines support prompt benzodiazepine rescue for convulsive status epilepticus. Route depends on available access and the approved plan, with airway monitoring essential.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A convulsion persists after appropriate benzodiazepine treatment. Which team-directed second-line options are supported by trial evidence?
choices: Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate, chosen for patient-specific risks
Only aspirin or heparin
Additional unsupervised oral benzodiazepines indefinitely
No further treatment until the EEG report is finalized
questions.explanation: The ESETT trial found broadly similar effectiveness among levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate for benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive status. Selection and monitoring are individualized.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Visible convulsions stop, but the patient remains unexpectedly unresponsive. What should the RN consider?
choices: Recovery is certain because shaking ended
Immediate oral feeding to test awareness
The event can no longer involve seizures
Nonconvulsive status or another complication; continue assessment and seek urgent team review
questions.explanation: Persistent impaired consciousness may reflect nonconvulsive seizures, medication effects, hypoxia, stroke, or metabolic problems. EEG and repeat clinical assessment may be needed.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which reversible factor should be checked promptly during a new seizure or status evaluation?
choices: The date of the next routine haircut
Capillary glucose, along with other cause-directed assessments
Only the patient's favorite foods
A single normal pulse recorded yesterday
questions.explanation: Hypoglycemia can trigger seizures and requires rapid detection. Further evaluation may include electrolytes, infection, medication adherence, withdrawal, and acute brain injury.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: After a seizure, a patient is confused and asks for water. Which nursing response is safest?
choices: Offer water before checking swallowing or alertness
Give several oral tablets to prevent another event
Continue airway and neurologic reassessment and wait until fully alert and safe to swallow before oral intake
Leave the patient alone because confusion is always brief
questions.explanation: Postictal confusion and possible aspiration risk require continued assessment. Food, fluids, and oral medication should wait until alertness and swallowing safety are established.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which discharge teaching best supports a patient with recurrent seizures?
choices: Use a written action plan, take prescribed medication consistently, review rescue steps, and follow individualized safety and driving advice
Stop antiseizure medicine whenever several seizure-free days pass
Assume every witness should restrain the patient's arms
Use one universal driving restriction regardless of local law
questions.explanation: An individualized action plan and medication adherence help prevent and respond to recurrence. Safety, rescue therapy, and driving guidance depend on the patient and local requirements.
